h1:
Koh Kood Local Food
Curry, Noodles & Bold One-Plate Stir-Fry
intro: Most food on Koh Kood costs more than on the mainland, because everything has to come over by boat. But if you know where the islanders eat, you can still get a filling one-plate meal starting at 50–70 THB. We've picked the local joints — stir-fry shops, rice-and-curry, noodles and Isaan places that villagers and island workers actually eat at — sorted by area so they're easy to track down.

blocks.html: Koh Kood sits at the far end of Thailand's eastern seaboard — a long trip out, with a drive to Trat and then a boat. So it's normal for food on the island to cost more than on the mainland. A plate at a resort restaurant usually starts at 150–250 THB, but if you head out to the local shops along the main road, prices drop to what island workers pay every day. This article rounds up one-plate meals, rice-and-curry, noodles and Isaan food that focus on filling and good value over a pretty view.

blocks.title: Read before you go
blocks.html: During the monsoon, May–October, the sea gets rough, several speedboat operators stop running, and some resorts and shops close for a long stretch. If you're going off-season, double-check that boats are still running and the place you want to eat is still open. In high season, November–April, it's busy and prices on goods and rooms go up.

blocks.text: Klong Chao — the hub for one-plate meals

blocks.html: Klong Chao is where most visitors stay. The Klong Chao waterfall and the concrete bridge in the middle of the village are the main landmarks — and around that bridge you'll find small stir-fry and noodle shops, all within walking distance of each other. It's the easiest place to start if you're staying nearby.

items.name: Cowboy
items.blurb: A stir-fry shop near the concrete bridge in the middle of Klong Chao. They do noodle soups and one-plate dishes like pad kaprao, prices are friendly, and some nights there's live music. It's a regular stop for people staying around Klong Chao.
items.meta: Klong Chao · near the village bridge

items.name: Thai Kitchen
items.blurb: A tiny stir-fry shop with just a couple of tables, cooked to order, easy on the wallet. Good for a quiet single meal with no long wait. It's in Klong Chao, walkable from a lot of the guesthouses.

items.name: ChalaOne
items.blurb: A canal-side shop with a short menu, cooked to order, known for its stewed pork-leg rice (khao kha moo) — soft and tender over rice. You can sit and eat by the water, and prices are still at the local level.

items.name: Aroi Aroi
items.blurb: A general Thai restaurant just before the Klong Chao waterfall junction, with seating by the canal and easygoing prices. An easy stop on the way to the waterfall — order a one-plate dish or share a few mains.
items.meta: Klong Chao · before the waterfall junction

blocks.title: Dinner tip
blocks.html: Near Klong Chao, on the road toward the waterfall, there's a moo kratha (Thai BBQ hotpot) place that's great for groups. Grilling your own works out cheaper than ordering several single plates, and the per-head price usually beats eating at a resort restaurant.

blocks.text: Mid-island (Hin Dam–Ao Tapao) — the real curry and Isaan spots

blocks.html: Drive from Klong Chao toward the middle of the island, around Hin Dam and the turnoff to Ao Tapao, and you hit the zone where the truly local shops cluster. They might look plain — concrete floors, wooden tables — but the cooking is real and the prices are good. This is the area where islanders eat among themselves, more than the tourist zone.

items.name: Esan Family
items.blurb: An Isaan shop near the Koh Kood pharmacy — som tam, sticky rice, grilled beef, plain wooden tables but bold, properly seasoned cooking. One of the best-value places in the middle of the island.

items.name: Isan Sab Noa by Pa Muan
items.blurb: A roadside Isaan shop near the mid-island junction, doing som tam and local dishes. Islanders stop here for lunch a lot — plates from 60 THB, a small place for a quick meal.

items.name: 108 (opposite the hospital)
items.blurb: The front looks like nothing much, but step in and sit at the plain tables and you'll find good Isaan food. It's across from the Koh Kood hospital and well known among people who work on the island.

items.name: Mid-island noodle shop
items.blurb: A small noodle shop in a concrete building mid-island. Standard, homey noodle soup at a cheap price — good for a light bite while you're driving around exploring the island.

blocks.text: The road to Ao Salad — kuay jab and village shops

blocks.html: The road to Ao Salad, in the north of the island, has local shops scattered along it, with fewer people than the Klong Chao area. The places out here are the real village shops at local prices — worth a stop if you're driving up toward the Ao Salad fishing village.

items.name: Kodmookrob
items.blurb: A kuay jab (rolled-noodle soup) shop in a wooden house set back from the road to Ao Salad, with broth and crispy pork. There's a vegetarian option too. It's a noodle shop that's different from the usual clear-broth noodle soups.
items.meta: Toward Ao Salad · wooden house off the road

items.name: Ton Kathin
items.blurb: A plain Thai restaurant opposite Mark & Meal on the Ao Salad road — a no-frills village shop. Order a one-plate dish or share some mains over rice. Local prices.
items.meta: Toward Ao Salad · opposite Mark & Meal

items.name: Lap Udon
items.blurb: An Isaan shop near the junction toward the southern resorts — larb, koi, grilled chicken. It reviews well among islanders, bold and properly Isaan, good ordered with sticky rice for dinner.
items.meta: South of Klong Chao · resort turnoff

items.name: The Table Local
items.blurb: An all-in-one stop — restaurant, mini-mart and a small fuel pump. They do curries and homey Thai one-plate dishes. Handy if you want to restock and grab a meal in one place.
items.meta: On the main road · mini-mart + fuel

blocks.title: About island prices
blocks.html: The prices in this article are rough ranges from reviews and may climb with the season and rising costs. Many local shops take cash only, and phone signal and internet are still limited in spots around the island, so carrying cash will save you some hassle.

If you have two days, here's an eating route built around local shops so you don't have to rely on resort restaurants for every meal. It's sorted by area so you can get around by motorbike or car easily. Drive carefully on the island — a lot of stretches are narrow and steep.

blocks.text: How to eat cheaply on Koh Kood

items: Leave the resort restaurant — eating in is convenient but pricey; head to the main road and prices drop right away
Go one-plate or moo kratha — single plates keep the budget tight, and Thai BBQ is good value if there are several of you
Carry cash — most local shops don't take transfers or cards, and there are few ATMs on the island
Avoid rushed meals in high season — small shops get busy and the wait is long; going before or after peak hours is easier
Ask villagers or your hotel staff — they know which shops are actually open that day, since some only open on certain days

blocks.text: More worth a stop if you get out that far

items.name: The Corner (Ao Ngam Kho)
items.blurb: A family shop above a small lagoon, doing curries and fragrant soups at local prices, with a lovely setting.

items.name: Junction (Huang Nam Kaeo waterfall / big tree junction)
items.blurb: A Thai restaurant right at the junction near the giant makha tree — a genuine village shop, an easy stop while you're out in nature.

items.name: Captain Nhong Seafood (Ao Salad)
items.blurb: A seafood spot in the Ao Salad fishing village, with bay views and fresh seafood. Not rock-bottom local prices, but worth it if you want one seafood meal.

faq.q: Is there cheap food on Koh Kood?
faq.a: Yes, but you have to leave the resort restaurants and eat at the shops along the main road. Stir-fry shops, rice-and-curry, noodles and Isaan places start at 50–70 THB a plate, while resort restaurants usually start at 150 THB and up — because goods have to come over by boat, so prices run higher than on the mainland overall.

faq.q: Which areas have the local shops on Koh Kood?
faq.a: There are three main areas: Klong Chao (one-plate and noodle shops around the village bridge), mid-island around Hin Dam–Ao Tapao (rice-and-curry and Isaan at genuinely local prices), and the road up to Ao Salad in the north (kuay jab and village shops).

faq.q: Do restaurants on Koh Kood take cards or transfers?
faq.a: Most local shops are cash only, ATMs on the island are scarce, and signal is limited in some spots. It's best to withdraw enough cash on the Trat mainland before you cross over.

faq.q: When should I visit Koh Kood to find everything open?
faq.a: November–April is high season, when shops are fully open but it's busy and prices go up. May–October is monsoon, with rough seas — some boat operators stop running and some shops and resorts close for long stretches. If you're going off-season, check the boats and the places you want to eat in advance.

faq.q: Where should I go for bold Isaan food on Koh Kood?
faq.a: Mid-island has Esan Family near the pharmacy and 108 opposite the hospital. South of Klong Chao there's Lap Udon, which reviews well for its larb and grilled chicken. All of them are spots where islanders eat among themselves.
